items.title: 22.6.2 Reactions of the Aromatic Ring in Phenols

source_refs.note: Topic 22.6.2 with Quick Check 22.5, answered (PDF 96-97); the equations are redrawn. The book's '2 phenol' nitration equation is given per molecule. The exercises (PDF 98-100) are not part of the lesson body. Answers need review.

blocks.text: The oxygen of phenol's -OH group donates electron density into the ring: one of its lone pairs overlaps with the ring's pi system and becomes delocalised. The extra electron density makes the ring more open to electrophilic attack (activated), and the -OH group directs incoming electrophiles to the 2, 4 and 6 positions.

Phenol is nitrated by dilute nitric acid at room temperature, giving a mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol: C6H5OH + HNO3 -> HOC6H4NO2 + H2O. With concentrated nitric acid the product is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol: C6H5OH + 3HNO3 -> C6H2(NO2)3OH + 3H2O. Benzene, by contrast, needs a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids warmed to between 25 and 60 C; phenol, being more reactive, needs milder conditions.

Phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature: it decolourises the orange bromine solution and forms a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol: C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr. Benzene is brominated only by pure bromine (not a solution) with an anhydrous AlBr3 catalyst; phenol reacts readily with bromine water and no catalyst.

1-naphthol has a hydroxyl group at position 1 of naphthalene. As in phenol, the -OH group donates electrons and activates the naphthalene ring to electrophilic substitution, directing electrophiles to positions 2 and/or 4; positions 9 and 10 cannot be substituted because they carry no hydrogen. With bromine in ethanoic acid, 1-naphthol gives 2-bromo-1-naphthol and 4-bromo-1-naphthol.

blocks.alt: Top: phenol with dilute HNO3 at room temperature gives 2-nitrophenol + 4-nitrophenol; with concentrated HNO3 it gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol. Middle: phenol + 3Br2(aq), orange, gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol, a white precipitate, + 3HBr; benzene needs pure bromine and AlBr3. Bottom: 1-naphthol with Br2 in ethanoic acid gives 2-bromo-1-naphthol + 4-bromo-1-naphthol.
blocks.caption: Nitration and bromination of phenol and 1-naphthol (original diagram after the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: Because the -OH group feeds electrons into the ring, phenol reacts with dilute reagents that leave benzene untouched, and the new groups go to the positions next to and opposite the -OH group. 1-naphthol behaves in the same way, at positions 2 and 4.

blocks.prompt: The reaction of phenol with bromine water is used to identify phenol. What is seen, and what is the systematic name of the product?
blocks.explanation: The orange bromine water is decolourised and a white precipitate forms: 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

blocks.prompt: Which is nitrated more easily, benzene or phenol, and why?
blocks.explanation: Phenol: a lone pair on its oxygen is delocalised into the ring, raising the electron density so the ring attracts electrophiles such as NO2+ more strongly; dilute nitric acid at room temperature is enough.

blocks.prompt: Write the equation for the nitration of 1-naphthol.
blocks.explanation: C10H7OH + HNO3 -> HOC10H6NO2 + H2O, giving 2-nitro-1-naphthol and 4-nitro-1-naphthol (by analogy with its bromination).

items: The -OH group activates the ring and directs to 2, 4 and 6.
Bromine water: white 2,4,6-tribromophenol (test for phenol); 1-naphthol reacts at 2 and 4.
